list.listitem: While often asymptomatic, men may have penile discharge, dysuria, or urethral pruritus and women may have abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, or intermenstrual vaginal bleeding. C
Screen all pregnant and nonpregnant women who are sexually active and younger than 25 years annually, as well as any women at high risk for infection. A

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all sexually-active men who have sex with men (MSM) for syphilis, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and HIV at least annually. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) found evidence for this recommendation to be insufficient based on their evidentiary standards. C
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) on endocervical, urethral, or urine samples are recommended over specimen culture tests. A

The CDC (2021) recommends treating suspected chlamydia infection of the cervix, urethra, rectum, or pharynx with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. If confirmed chlamydia infection, or if pregnant, a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally is appropriate. If gonococcal infection has not been ruled out, also give ceftriaxone 500 mg as a single IM dose (1 gram if >300 pounds).A

background.definition: Urogenital chlamydia is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

list.listitem: In 2022, a total of 1.65 million cases of chlamydial infection were reported to the CDC in 50 states and the District of Columbia for a rate of 495 cases per 100,000 population. The infection rate is higher among women than men likely reflecting a larger number of women screened for chlamydia; however, in men, the rate increased by 32% between 2015 and 2019. Since 2019, rates decreased from 395 to 361 per 100,000 in 2022.
In 2022, 57.7% of chlamydia infections were among persons between age 15 and 24 years.

Based on electronic data from Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, Australia, of the 1,295 first presentations of acute non-gonococcal urethritis, 32% had C. trachomatis and 11% had M. genitalium detected. Rates of chlamydia urethritis were higher in men who have sex with women than MSM.

The rate of chlamydia urethritis attributable to oral sex was 2.7% in a case-control study of MSM; men reported the oropharynx as their only urethral exposure in the past 60 days in 31.4% of chlamydial urethritis cases in this population from a Seattle sexually-transmitted disease (STD) clinic.

In a report of rectal screening for chlamydia in over 3,000 men presenting to a London STI clinic, 8.2% were positive; most of these men (69.2%) were asymptomatic and would have been missed without routine screening.

Among 4727 patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), 397 (8.4%) had 881 chlamydia infections and 331 had 861 gonococcal infections for an incidence rate of 2.95 and 2.88 per 100 person-years, respectively, based on 2007-2017 medical record data from HIV Outpatient Study participants receiving care at HIV clinics.
Most cases are undiagnosed. The CDC estimates that 2.8 million of cases of chlamydia occur each year.

According to the CDC, in 2022, reported cases of chlamydial infection were higher among Black vs. White persons (468,384 and 361,722 cases, respectively) and higher among Black or White persons than Hispanic persons (234,276 cases).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies of diverse populations of women attending sexual health services found a concurrent rectal chlamydia infection rate of 68.1% among those who tested positive for urogenital chlamydia (95% CI 56.6%-79.6%) and 2.2% among those who tested negative for urogenital chlamydia (95% CI 0%-5.2%). A report of anal intercourse was not associated with presence of rectal chlamydia.

In a study of the Netherlands general population (1996 to 2017), overall CT seroprevalence was 10.5% (95% CI 9.2% to 12.0%) in women and 5.8% (95% CI: 4.7% to 7.0%) in men. Rates were non-significantly increased among women <25 years and significantly decreased from 15.6% in 1996 to 11.2% in 2017 among older women.

Based on visit data for MSM tested for GC and CT at 30 STD clinics, of 139,718 test visits, overall positivity for chlamydia was 13.3% (95% CI 12.7-13.9). Urethral positivity was 5.2%, rectal positivity 12.6%, and pharyngeal positivity 1.8%. In a Japanese study, the prevalence of rectal chlamydia among HIV-negative MSM compared to an HIV-positive MSM cohort was 16.4% and 15.9%, respectively.

In a cohort study of 764 transgender women in Thailand, 232 (30.4%) had chlamydia or gonorrhea infections at any anatomical site, with an overall incidence of 23.7 per 100 person-years. Rectal chlamydia infections occurred in 19.5%. Among transgender women in Brazil, prevalence rates of anorectal CT or NG and/or CT or gonorrhea were lower at 8.9% and 15.2%, respectively; most (88.9% for CT) were asymptomatic.
The medical costs of all STIs are estimated at more than $16 billion per year in the United States.
Chlamydia is the most common STI in the world. Chlamydia infection can facilitate HIV infection.
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU).

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), a sequalae of untreated chlamydia infection in women, can lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. Authors of a meta-analysis found CT-specific IgG was associated with a 2-fold increased risk of tubal-factor infertility.

Chlamydia infection can lead to adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm labor, miscarriage, and stillbirth. Adverse infant outcomes linked to chlamydia exposure include pneumonia and ophthalmia neonatorum which can cause blindness.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 25 studies with 11960 subjects found an association between chlamydia infections and ectopic pregnancy with an odds ratio (OR) of 3.03, 95% CI 2.37-3.89.
Chlamydia trachomatis infection increases the risk for ovarian cancer (OR 1.3; 95%CI 1.2-1.5) based on a review of 18 studies including 8207 patients.
Urogenital chlamydia infections are caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, which is a small gram-negative bacterium.

In a study of 155 men with NGU and 103 controls, 12% of those with NGU had mixed pathogens, primarily chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium; none of the control patients had either of these pathogens identified.
The bacterium lives as an obligatory parasite.
The incubation period is 5 to 7 days after exposure.
Chlamydia tends to infect the endocervical canal in women and the urethra in men; rectal infection can occur in those who practice anal intercourse.

Urethritis is primarily due to infectious agents ascending from the periurethral skin and distal urethra. Hematogenous spread can also occur. Whether infection occurs is based on multiple factors including pathogenicity of the agent, inoculum size, and host defenses (including genetic factors).

Long-term infection and inflammation can lead to cell proliferation, tissue remodeling, and scarring; in genetically-predisposed individuals, persistent infection/inflammation is linked to the onset of autoimmune responses.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies did not find any difference in the microbial biodiversity between CT-positive and healthy women. In another meta-analysis of 6 studies, however, Lactobacillus (L.) iners-dominated vaginal microbiotas were associated with 3.4-fold higher odds of CT compared with L. crispatus -dominated microbiotas.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Age 25 years and older and at increased risk for infection
History of exchanging sex for money or drugs
Sex partner with a sexually transmitted infection (STI)
Member of a population with increased prevalence of STI (American Indian/Alaska Native, Black, Hispanic/Latinx, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander)
Concurrent other STI or history of STI

list.listitem: The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening all women ages 21-24 who are sexually active. B

The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening all women older than age 25 who are sexually active and who are at increased risk for infection, regardless of whether they are symptomatic. Risk factors are listed above. B
The USPSTF (2021) concludes that there is insufficient evidence regarding screening in men, though men in certain high-risk groups may be considered for screening. I
The CDC recommends screening all sexually-active MSM for syphilis, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and HIV at least annually. C
The USPSTF (2020) recommends intensive behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. B

For primary prevention, condoms and behavioral counseling are recommended to prevent transmission of the infection. Doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis can reduce the risk of new infection in high-risk patients. B

The USPSTF (2021) recommends screening of all sexually active nonpregnant and pregnant women 21-24 years and women over age 25 who are at increased risk for chlamydia. Risk factors are listed above. This recommendation also applies to persons who are asymptomatic.
Chlamydia screening in young women may reduce the incidence of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend screening in men.
One study found differences in screening based on age, race, and insurance status, so a systematic approach is likely needed for optimal screening.

In a cluster RCT of opportunistic screening for chlamydia among individuals aged 16 to 29 years attending primary care clinics in Australia, chlamydia prevalence decreased by a similar amount for intervention and control clinics (from 5% and 4.6%, respectively to 3.4% and 3.4%).
The CDC recommends screening all sexually-active MSM for syphilis, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and HIV at least annually.

In a case series of 489 female sex-workers undergoing STI screening, 5.1% were positive for chlamydia, 2.0% were positive for gonorrhea and 1.4% were coinfected. Sampling from the vagina only was shown to miss 40% of CT infections and 60% of NG infections compared to pooled sampling from three sites – pharyngeal, vaginal, and rectal.

A practice-based intervention including education, practical resources (e.g., targets, posters), and up to two additional contacts resulted in higher screening rates than in control practices (post-intervention rates 3.46/100 vs. 2.82/100, respectively).

In an emergency department RCT, a brief intervention did not increase the percentage of women accepting an offer of screening for STIs among 18- to 35-year-old women who had sex with men but were not presenting for STI testing or treatment (48% vs. 36% among controls). Of the 71 asymptomatic women tested, five (7%) tested positive for chlamydia.

Strategies that increase STI screening rates among MSM include regular serological screening for syphilis during routine human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) care, syphilis serology included with blood tests performed as part of HIV monitoring, use of an electronic medical record computer alert, and an electronic medical record system to enhance syphilis retesting after syphilis treatment.

In one Chinese study of 300 MSM, both free testing and free testing with pay-it-forward (pay for the next person to be tested) improved chlamydia and gonorrhea screening over fee-for-service testing of US$22 (56%, 46% and 18%, respectively).
Using a condom to avoid exposure is the best means of primary prevention.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found that condom communication with the partner and intention to use condoms were predictors of future condom use among adolescents. Teens who used a condom with their first sexual experience were more likely to continue to do so.
Periodic presumptive treatment is effective in reducing prevalence of gonorrhea, chlamydia, and ulcerative STIs among sex workers, based on results of a systematic review.

Among high-risk MSM, postexposure prophylaxis with 200 mg of doxycycline within 24 to 72 hours of exposure reduced the risk of new STIs (22% vs. 42%; number needed to treat (NNT) = 6.8; 95% CI 3.8-37.0). Benefit was demonstrated for chlamydia and syphilis but not for gonorrheal infection. This was confirmed in an RCT including 501 men who have sex with men and transgender women and were either using preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP; n = 327) or were living with human immunodeficiency virus. In this study, postexposure prophylaxis with 200 mg of doxycycline within 24 to 72 hours of exposure reduced risk of STIs at 9 months for both for the PrEP group (10.7% vs 31.9%; NNT = 5) and the group living with HIV (11.8% vs 30.5%; NNT = 5). Similiar results were found in a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis including patients at risk for infection (73% MSM).

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that vaginal tenofovir microbicides, but not other types of topical microbicides, may reduce the risk of acquisition of HIV and herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infections in women. In one RCT, use of vaginal microbicides BufferGel and PRO2000 vs. placebo gel had no protective effect against chlamydia, gonorrhea, or trichomoniasis.
There is good evidence that nonoxynol-9 does not protect against STIs, including gonorrhea (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.67-1.24).

The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence and authors of a meta-analysis concluded that the balance of evidence marginally supports counseling intervention to reduce and prevent STIs. Interventions including multiple sessions may be most effective.

The USPSTF (2020) recommends intensive behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. Interventions involving >120 minutes of counseling, delivered over several sessions, have the strongest effect.

In the evidence report supporting this recommendation, absolute differences in STI acquisition between groups ranged from 19% fewer to 4% more people acquiring STI; the variation was explained by differences in baseline population STI risk and intervention effectiveness. Of the 34 trials with 21,417 primarily heterosexual adolescents and young adults 12 to 25 years, interventions were associated with self-reported behavioral change (e.g., increased condom use) that reduce STI risk (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.10-1.56).

Evidence supporting one-to-one counseling for STI prevention is mixed. In an RCT of 5012 adults presenting for HIV testing to STD clinics, intensive risk-reduction counseling did not reduce STIs over the subsequent 6 months (12.3% vs. 11.1% for standard care group). Counseling resulted in less self-reported unprotected sex with nonprimary partners and lower numbers of total partners.
Counseling provided to young Black men improved correct condom use but did not have a significant effect on chlamydia and gonorrhea incidence.

Brief telephone counseling provided every 8 weeks for 36 months slightly reduced incident chlamydial infections by 1.5% among African American adolescent girls aged 14 to 20 years (94/342 vs. 104/359 participants) but not gonorrhea infections.
The prevention intervention Many Men, Many Voices HIV/ STD has been successful in reducing high-risk sexual behaviors and increasing protective behaviors among black MSM.

A novel chlamydia vaccine based on a recombinant protein subunit (CTH522) has undergone phase I testing. In a 3-arm phase I RCT with 35 women aged 19-45 years randomly assigned to intervention or placebo (15 to CTH522 adjuvanted with CAF01 liposomes, 15 to CTH522 adjuvanted with aluminum hydroxide and 5 to placebo), 32 (91%) received all five vaccinations (3 intramuscular and 2 intranasal over 5 months) and all participants were included in the intention-to-treat analyses. Both vaccines were immunogenic in all patients, although the vaccine containing CAFO1 has a better immunogenic profile. Mild local injection-site reactions occurred in all intervention subjects and there were no serious adverse effects.

In an RCT including 3123 participants, an intervention including a series of text messages to improve sexual behaviors did not reduce chlamydia and gonorrhea reinfections at one year in people aged 16-24 years.
While often asymptomatic, men may have penile discharge, dysuria, or urethral pruritus and women may have abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, or intermenstrual vaginal bleeding. C
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) on endocervical, urethral, or urine samples are recommended over specimen culture tests. B
Point-of-care chlamydia testing is available but should be reserved for cases in which follow-up is unlikely. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Symptoms can be similar and clinical presentation can not always distinguish between them
Vaginal discharge is generally a gray color with a "fishy" odor
Vaginal discharge is usually thick and white with external genitalia irritation
Women have thin, grayish vaginal discharge; men usually are asymptomatic
Pelvic and/or abdominal pain with fever, nausea/vomiting

list.listitem: A sexual history should include 6-month risk assessment (number of partners, frequency of sexual activity, partner gender and their symptom status, orogenital sex, use of sex toys, and sex with persons who use illicit substances).

Infections in men may be asymptomatic. If symptomatic, symptoms of penile discharge, dysuria, or urethral pruritus typically occur 5 days to 10 days after exposure. Occasionally, the infection will ascend to the epididymis and cause pain and discomfort in that area. Mucopurulent or watery discharge from the penis may be present; if not, milking the shaft of the penis may produce the discharge.

Infections in women may be asymptomatic. If symptomatic, symptoms can include mucopurulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, and intermenstrual vaginal bleeding (e.g., bleeding after sex). Lower genital tract infections in women can ascend to the upper genital tract and cause PID and, rarely, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). Physical examination will show mucopurulent discharge from the endocervical canal and cervical friability. If PID is present, cervical motion tenderness and/or adnexal mass may be present.

Look for signs of atrophic changes in women and ulcers, warts, or other lesions in both men and women. Examine the urethra for signs of inflammation of the meatus, edema, or tenderness. Structural abnormalities such as urethral caruncle, urethral diverticulum, cystocele, urethrocele, rectocele, uterine, or mucosal prolapse may be detected.
A prospective study of 288 women found that adding pelvic examination to the history does not improve diagnostic accuracy.

The NAAThas replaced culture techniques for evaluating for gonococcal infections. The test has good sensitivity (92%-96%) and specificity (94%-99%). The NAAT can be performed on endocervical, urethral, or urine samples with similar sensitivity and specificity.

The 2021 CDC recommendation for laboratory-based detection is to use NAATs to detect chlamydia and gonorrhea. Optimal urogenital specimen types for chlamydia screening using NAAT include first-catch urine (for men) and vaginal swabs (for women). Exceptions include cases of child sexual assault involving boys, rectal and oropharyngeal infections in prepubescent girls, and when evaluating a potential gonorrhea treatment failure; in these cases, culture and susceptibility testing may be required. They note that self-collected vaginal swab specimens are equivalent in sensitivity and specificity to those collected by a clinician using NAATs and that women find this screening strategy highly acceptable.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 28 studies (unreported methodology) found the overall sensitivity for detecting chlamydia, gonorrhea, or trichomonas in women was greater with vaginal samples than urine samples (for chlamydia – sensitivity 0.94 (0.93 - 0.95) and 0.87 (0.86 - 0.88), respectively).
The 2016 European guideline recommends obtaining a culture before treatment in patients with a positive NAAT for gonorrhea.
As male urethral swabs are painful, urine testing is the preferred testing method; if direct sampling is desired, a plastic loop appears to be less painful than a rayon or Dacron swab.

The Bio-Rad Dx CT/NG/MG appears to be both highly sensitive and specific for the simultaneous detection of C. trachomatis, M. genitalium and N. gonorrhoeae in urogenital specimens of symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals.

Samples from SurePath liquid-based Pap can also be tested for chlamydia and gonorrhea; in one case series of 394 women (of whom C. trachomatis was present in 8.9%, and N. gonorrhoeae in 1.5%), all testing assays showed high specificity although sensitivity was highest for chlamydia on Aptima Combo 2 assay.

A positive leukocyte esterase or more than 10 white blood cells (WBC) per high-power field suggest an infectious cause of urethritis in men, but is not accurate in women. Infections should still be confirmed using NAAT.

Urinary white cell counts of >29 using rapid automated urine flow cytometry of first void was similarly sensitive but more specific for predicting C. trachomatis or M. genitalium infection than gram stain (81.5% and 85.8% compared with 86.8% and 64.7%, respectively).

Among men, a cut-off point of 12.5 urinary white cells/μl resulted in a sensitivity of 86.9% and specificity of 88.6% for predicting chlamydial infection in asymptomatic men, whose female sexual partners had been diagnosed as having a genital chlamydial infection.

Point-of-care testing by way of GeneXpert CT/NG has been reported as having concordance with conventional NAATs. In a study conducted in South Africa, point-of-care vs. centralized testing resulted in more prompt STI management.

The Cobas CT/NG v2.0 test using urogenital swabs, urine, and cervical cytology samples collected in PreservCyt solution was found to be highly sensitive. Depending on specimen type in women, the sensitivity ranged from 91.2% to 97.6%. Sensitivity was 98.4% in urine samples from males. Specificity ranged from 99.2% to 99%.

Evaluation of two rapid tests, the Chlamydia Rapid Test and the ACON Chlamydia Rapid Test Device, revealed that both tests performed below the levels stated by the manufacturers. Sensitivities were lower in men than women, and resulted in a high proportion of false-negative tests. One study found that a 90-min point-of-care test was not acceptable to the vast majority (91.5%) of clinic attendees and would not have influenced treatment rates or inappropriate prescribing; 20-minute tests showed only marginal benefit.

Authors of a systematic review of nine studies also found a lack of sufficient sensitivity for eight antigen detection tests (53%, 37% and 63% for cervical swabs, vaginal swabs and male urine) to recommend them as screening tests. However, the two studies of near-patient NAATs for all specimen types had a sensitivity of >98% and specificity of 99.4% making them acceptable for screening but requiring electricity and 90 minutes to perform in addition to being costly.
Gram stain of cervical discharge has very low sensitivity but excellent specificity. WBCs on gram stain have neither good sensitivity or specificity for the diagnosis of chlamydia.

Gram stain of the pharynx and rectum in asymptomatic men and women are not sufficiently sensitive to rule out infection. In one study, gram stain (5 or more WBC per hpf) in the diagnosis of culture positive urethritis in men had a sensitivity, specificity and positive likelihood ratio of 26% (95% CI 18-33), 91% (95% CI 87-94) and 2.7 (95% CI 1.8-4.2), respectively. The sensitivity of Gram stain to C. trachomatis was lower than for gonorrhea (23% vs. 80%).
Culture, nucleic acid hybridization tests, or a NAAT is required to rule out gonorrhea infection in these areas. NAAT is often preferred because it can be done with urine rather than swab.
For women with vaginal discharge, assess the discharge for color, consistency, odor, and pH measurement; consider a saline and potassium hydroxide preparation (wet prep) to diagnose vaginitis.
Asymptomatic infection is common among men and women. Men may report penile discharge or dysuria, while women may report abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, and intermenstrual vaginal bleeding.
Mucopurulent endocervical exudate can be visible in the endocervical canal, or cervical friability can be seen on physical examination.

STI Treatment Guidelines from the CDC recommend that for the diagnosis of urethritis, patients should have physical signs (dysuria, urethral pruritis, mucopurulent or purulent urethral discharge) or positive laboratory testing (e.g., Gram stain (preferred), positive leukocyte esterase test on first-void urine or microscopic examination of first-void urine sediment demonstrating ≥10 WBC per high-power field).
If chlamydia infection is suspected, NAAT testing should be performed on secretions from the urethra, urine, or endocervical canal.
Use empiric therapy for those testing positive for chlamydia with azithromycin or doxycycline before test results return.

Treat women with urethritis suspected of having an STI for both gonorrhea and chlamydia with single-dose ceftriaxone (500 mg IM) AND oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 7 days); obtain a pregnancy test before using tetracycline.

The CDC (2021) recommends treating suspected chlamydia infection of the cervix, urethra, rectum, or pharynx with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. If confirmed chlamydia infection or if pregnant a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally is appropriate.A

If gonococcal infection has not been ruled out, patients should receive ceftriaxone 500 mg as a single IM dose (1 gram if >300 pounds). If ceftriaxone is not available or if allergy, and gonococcal infection has not been excluded, the alternative regimen is gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 grams orally as a single dose. A

Treat suspected chlamydia infection of the cervix, urethra, pharynx and/or rectum with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. If confirmed chlamydia infection, or if pregnant, a single dose of azithromycin 1 gram orally is appropriate. If gonococcal infection has not been ruled out, also give ceftriaxone 500 mg as a single IM dose (1 gram if >300 pounds).
Compared to single-dose azithromycin, a 7-day doxycycline regimen increases the rate of microbiologic cure in MSM with asymptomatic rectal chlamydia infection.

Authors of a Cochrane review on antibiotics for urogenital chlamydia infection concluded that regimens with azithromycin are probably less effective than doxycycline for microbiological failure in men but there is little or no difference for clinical failure. For women, it was unclear whether there was a difference in either failure rate. Azithromycin probably slightly reduces adverse events compared to doxycycline.

If ceftriaxone is not available, the recommended alternative regimen is gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 grams orally as a single dose. A second alternative is cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose. As with ceftriaxone, if chlamydia has not been excluded give doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, and if pregnant, azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose.

In one RCT of 125 patients with untreated gonorrhea and chlamydia, ceftriaxone plus doxycycline was superior to cefixime plus doxycycline for the treatment of this co-infection (OR 4.4, 95% CI 1.1-25.7).

The 2015 UK National Guideline on the management of non-gonococcal urethritis cautions that 1 g azithromycin may result in antimicrobial resistance in M. genitalium and that neither azithromycin nor doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 7 days) achieves a cure rate of >90% for this microorganism.

The 2016 European guideline no longer recommends 1g azithromycin as first-line treatment due to concerns about this antimicrobial resistance. They recommend either doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days or an extended course of azithromycin with 500 mg initially followed by 250 mg daily for four day.s

Authors of a review of antimicrobial resistance patterns noted that although in vitro resistance has been reported, surveillance data suggest that clinically-significant resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines is rare. They note, however, that M. genitalium exhibits resistance to many antibiotics and that resistance to both first- and second-line agents (macrolides and fluoroquinolones) is increasing worldwide.

A meta-analysis in 2002 comparing azithromycin and doxycycline in the treatment of genital chlamydial infections showed that the treatments were equally effective, with microbial cure rates of 97% for azithromycin and 98% for doxycycline. However, in a recent RCT of adolescents incarcerated in a youth correctional facility who tested positive for chlamydia, there were no treatment failures in those randomized to receive doxycycline and seven treatment failures in those randomized to azithromycin (6/102 males and 1/53 females). Similarly, the microbiological anorectal cure rate was significantly lower among women who received a single dose of azithromycin than among those who received a 1-week course of doxycycline (85% vs. 94%, respectively); reported treatment-related adverse effect rates were similar. These higher failure rates should be balanced against greater convenience and likely better adherence with azithromycin.

Alternate regimens include 7 days of the following: erythromycin base 500 mg 4 times per day OR erythromycin ethylsuccinate 800 mg 4 times per day OR ofloxacin 300 mg twice per day OR levofloxacin 500 mg once per day.

The World Health Organization recommends that MSM who report unprotected receptive anal intercourse and either multiple partners or a partner with a STI in the past 6 months be presumptively treated for asymptomatic rectal gonorrhea and chlamydia. In testing this approach in Kenya, the NNT in order to treat one infection was four among asymptomatic MSM who meet these criteria for presumptive treatment.

A 2025 cohort study found approximately 75% of patients with positive chlamydia tests received documented treatment within 30 days and 14% of patients with positive tests received the recommended first-line therapy, doxycycline.

Treat partners (within the preceding 60 days) of women with STIs or refer them for treatment. Familiarize yourself with state regulations and CDC advice governing whether partners may be treated without direct examination.

One study found that treating partners immediately (through medication given directly to patients or offering medications to partners without seeing them) resulted in fewer gonococcal infections (but not chlamydial infections) at follow-up (3% vs. 11%; NNT = 12.5).

In a 3-arm RCT, the proportions of contactable partners considered treated within 6 weeks of index diagnosis were 39/111 (35%) for telephone assessment of partner(s) plus standard partner notification, 46/100 (46%) for community pharmacist assessment of partner(s) plus routine partner notification and 46/102 (45%) for standard partner notification (patient referral) alone. All of these care models were deemed acceptable.
Severe cases of pelvic inflammatory disease warrant hospitalization for parenteral antibiotic therapy.
Urethral stricture may be a consequence of urethritis, especially gonococcal urethritis. When stricture is present, urology referral is warranted.
Infertility or subsequent ectopic pregnancy can also be late complications of STIs.
Treatment provides a high percentage of cure: 97% with azithromycin and 98% with doxycycline. B

Test of cure for chlamydia and gonococcal urethritis following completion of recommended therapy is only recommended for pregnant women (3-4 weeks after treatment) or if mediation non-adherence is suspected, symptoms persist, or reinfection occurs. C
Consider retesting after 3 months due to the potential for reinfection from an untreated partner. B
Untreated infection in men can cause an ascending infection in the epididymis.
Untreated infection in women can cause PID or, rarely, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

Spontaneous clearance of infection can occur. In one study of 482 heterosexual men and women ≥18 years of age visiting an STI clinic between 2011 and 2013 for whom retesting was conducted prior to treatment, clearance of chlamydia occurred in 9.1% (10/110) for urine specimens, 6.8% (20/292) for vaginal swab specimens, 12.7% (8/63) for anorectal swab specimens.
Treatment provides a high percentage of cure: 97% with azithromycin and 98% with doxycycline.
In a study on patient adherence to filling prescriptions for chlamydia treatment given in the ED, 82.4% picked up their doxycycline prescription.

Test of cure (TOC), except for pregnant women, is not recommended unless symptoms persist, medication adherence is uncertain, or reinfection is suspected. If TOC is indicated, this should be performed as early as 3 weeks following treatment completion.

Reinfection is common particularly in the period immediately after treatment and patients should be advised of such risk. Consider retesting after 3 months because of the potential for reinfection from an untreated partner.

With respect to treatment failure, investigators from the Sexually Transmitted Bacteria Reference Unit at Public Health England recruited 147 individuals with chlamydia or gonorrhea infections and asked them to return nine self-taken samples from the site of infection over a course of 35 days. They found that the median time to clearance of gonorrhea infection was 4 days (IQR 2-10 days) and 10 days (IQR 7-14 days) for chlamydia infection. Vaginal chlamydia infections took longer to clear as did gonorrhea infection in MSM

If rescreening is needed, use of home-based, self-obtained vaginal swabs (kits mailed to the home) resulted in significant increases in rescreening rates compared with rescreening in either an STD or family planning clinic.
There is a small increase in subsequent PID following chlamydia infection (0.15 vs. 0.08 per 100 person-years) for those with negative chlamydia tests).
NAAT testing performed less than 3 weeks after successful therapy could lead to a false positive result due to dead organisms.
Avoid sexual contact for at least 7 days after completion of therapy.
Partner notification and treatment offers have been shown to have a positive influence on recurrence rates.
Screening for HIV should be offered to all patients who have an STI.
Condom use has been shown to reduce the risk for chlamydial infections.

Prenatal screening in pregnant women can prevent chlamydia infection among neonates. Adverse pregnancy outcomes that can be caused by chlamydial infection include: miscarriage, premature rupture of membranes, preterm labor, low birth weight, stillbirth and infant mortality.
Azithromycin (1 g orally in single dose) is safe in pregnancy and is considered first-line therapy.
Another alternative is amoxicillin 500 mg 3 times per day for 7 days.
Treatment with azithromycin or clindamycin is associated with fewer side effects than erythromycin.
The CDC recommends retesting at 3 weeks after completion of therapy to document chlamydial eradication and again 3 months later.
Doxycycline, ofloxacin, and levofloxacin are contraindicated during pregnancy.
